title: Jonathan's Faith and Saul's Rash Oath
summary: While Saul waits under a pomegranate tree, Jonathan and his armor-bearer climb alone to a Philistine outpost, trusting that the LORD can save by many or by few. Their attack sets off a panic that becomes a rout, and the LORD saves Israel that day. But Saul's oath forbidding food weakens his troops, drives them to eat meat with the blood, and nearly costs Jonathan his life, until the people ransom him. The chapter closes with a summary of Saul's wars and family.
story: Chapter 13 left Israel cornered: a vast Philistine army at Michmash, six hundred Israelites with Saul, and hardly a sword among them. Samuel had just told Saul his kingdom would not endure. Chapter 14 sets two ways of leading side by side. Jonathan acts in bold faith and God works through him. Saul stays put, then starts religious actions he doesn't finish, swears a foolish oath, and is ready to execute his own son to keep it. The victory is real and it is the LORD's, but the chapter shows the king becoming an obstacle to the very deliverance he was anointed to bring. The closing summary (verses 47 to 52) credits Saul with real military success before chapter 15 records his final rejection.
historical:
The setting is the Michmash pass in the land of Benjamin, where a steep wadi separates Geba on the south from Michmash on the north. The two crags Bozez and Seneh stood on either side of that pass, and travelers and scholars have long identified the gorge with the modern Wadi Suweinit. The battle moves west from Michmash to Aijalon, down toward the coastal plain where the Philistines lived. Verse 21 mentions Hebrews who had been serving in the Philistine camps and who now changed sides. Many scholars think "Hebrews" here refers to people connected to Israel but not fully identified with it, living under Philistine control.

Ahijah the priest links this scene to the fallen house of Eli: he is a great-grandson of Eli, whose line was condemned in chapter 2. In verse 18 the traditional Hebrew text has Saul call for "the ark of God," but the ark had been at Kiriath-jearim since chapter 7, and the Greek translation reads "ephod." Many translators and commentators think the ephod is meant, since it was the instrument used to seek God's guidance. Verse 41 is another textual question: the BSB follows the fuller Greek text, which names the Urim and Thummim, while the shorter Hebrew text is harder to read.
cultural:
The ephod in this context was a priestly garment that held the Urim and Thummim, sacred objects used to receive a yes or no answer from God (Exodus 28:30). No one knows exactly what they looked like or how they worked; the text tells only that they gave a decision between two options. When Saul tells the priest to withdraw his hand, he is breaking off the consultation mid-way because events are moving too fast. Casting lots (verse 42) was a similar means of letting God decide, used for example to divide the land and to identify Achan in Joshua 7.

Oaths were taken with deadly seriousness. A curse spoken in God's name was believed to bind the one who swore it and those placed under it. That is why the soldiers refuse the honey, why Saul thinks the oath explains God's silence, and why he feels bound to kill Jonathan. The law forbade eating meat with its blood (Leviticus 17:10-14; Deuteronomy 12:23-24), because the life is in the blood; blood was to be drained out and poured on the ground. The large stone in verse 33 served as a place to slaughter animals properly. Saul's altar there is noted as his first, a detail that may be meant as a quiet comment on how late he came to it.
literary: The chapter is built on contrasts. It opens with Jonathan saying "Come, let us cross over" while Saul sits under a tree. Jonathan asks for a sign and acts; Saul consults the priest and then stops him. Jonathan's words about God (verse 6) are the theological heart of the chapter; Saul's words are mostly oaths and commands. The honey episode turns the victory story into a court case, with the lot moving from the people, to Saul and Jonathan, to Jonathan alone, a sequence that recalls Achan's discovery in Joshua 7. Jonathan's verdict, "My father has brought trouble to the land," uses the verb for trouble that names the Valley of Achor where Achan was judged (Joshua 7:25-26), so the reader is invited to ask who the real troubler of Israel is. The chapter ends with an archival summary of wars and family, a common way for the historian to close a king's main account.

outline.t: Jonathan sets out; Saul waits under the pomegranate tree
Jonathan and his armor-bearer climb to the outpost
Panic in the Philistine camp; the LORD saves Israel
Exhausted troops eat meat with the blood; Saul's altar
God's silence, the lot, and the people's ransom of Jonathan
Summary of Saul's wars, family, and army

doctrines.note: "Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few." The narrator agrees: "the LORD saved Israel that day." Salvation in Samuel is first of all rescue from enemies, and it is always God's act, whatever human instruments he uses.

Jonathan's faith is bold but not presumptuous. He says "perhaps," asks for a sign, and trusts God's power rather than any guarantee of his own success. Faith here is confidence in who God is, acted on with humility.

The soldiers' eating of blood shows how a leader's unwise rule can push people into breaking God's actual law. Saul's man-made oath is enforced ruthlessly while God's command is trampled, a pattern Jesus later rebukes in those who set aside God's commands for their own traditions.

words.note: Yasha, to save or deliver. It appears in Jonathan's confession (verse 6), in the narrator's summary (verse 23), and in Saul's oath by "the LORD who saves Israel" (verse 39). The name Joshua, and its later Greek form Jesus, is built from this root.

Yeshuah, salvation or deliverance. The people use it of Jonathan's victory in verse 45, which the BSB renders "great deliverance." They see that Jonathan was God's instrument, which is why they refuse to let him die.

Padah, to ransom or redeem. The BSB says the people "rescued" Jonathan, but the verb normally means to redeem by paying a price or providing a substitute. Some scholars think an animal or payment was given in his place; others take it more generally as deliverance. The text does not say how.

Akar, to trouble. Jonathan says his father has brought trouble on the land. It is the same verb used of Achan, who brought trouble on Israel by breaking a sacred ban (Joshua 7:25). The echo turns the lot scene around: the king, not the son, is the true troubler.

christ: Jonathan's confession that the LORD can save "by many or by few" states a pattern that runs through Scripture: God delivers his people through weakness, so that the victory is plainly his. That pattern reaches its fullest form in the cross, where salvation comes through one man who is rejected and killed. The chapter also shows the danger of a leader who binds heavy burdens on others and keeps the letter of an oath while breaking the heart of God's law, something Jesus confronts directly (Mark 7:8-13). And there is a thematic echo, not a prediction, in the picture of a king's son who wins deliverance for Israel and is sentenced to die by his father's word. In Jonathan the people refuse the death. In the gospel the Father gives the Son, and the Son is not spared, so that others may be redeemed.

hard.q: Did God really answer through a lot and point to Jonathan, as if his innocent honey-eating were a sin?
hard.a: The chapter raises the question honestly. The lot did single out Jonathan, and God was silent to Saul. Readers take this in different ways. Some think the lot simply identified who had broken the oath, as a factual matter, without God endorsing Saul's oath or its penalty; Jonathan was technically guilty under a rash vow he never heard. Others emphasize that God's silence came first, and that it was a judgment on Saul's whole conduct (the broken-off consultation, the foolish oath, the troops driven to sin), so that the lot exposes Saul's folly more than Jonathan's fault. On either reading the narrator clearly sides with Jonathan and the people: Jonathan acted "with God's help," and the oath that would have killed him is shown to be Saul's error, not God's will.

questions: Jonathan said, "Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf." How does his mix of boldness and humility compare with the way you approach risks for God?
Saul's oath sounded zealous but left his soldiers faint and led them into sin. Where can religious intensity become a burden God never asked for?
The people stood up to the king to save Jonathan. When is it right to resist a leader's word, and how would you know?
